headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of Hair and Scalp
headings.content:
Hair is composed primarily of a tough protein called **keratin**, growing from follicles embedded in the dermis layer of the skin. The visible portion above the skin surface is the hair shaft, while the part beneath is the root, ending in the hair bulb where living cells actively divide. The scalp contains numerous sebaceous glands that secrete **sebum**, an oily substance that lubricates the hair and skin. Normal scalp pH is slightly acidic, which helps prevent bacterial and fungal growth.

- **Anagen phase**: The active growth phase lasting several years.
- **Catagen phase**: A short transitional phase lasting a few weeks.
- **Telogen phase**: The resting phase before hair shedding occurs.

headings.title: Assessment of Hair and Scalp Health
headings.content: A systematic nursing assessment of the hair and scalp begins with inspection and gentle palpation. Nurses examine the scalp for lesions, scaling, erythema, tenderness, and signs of infestation like lice or nits. Hair texture, distribution, and overall cleanliness provide important clues about a patient's nutritional status, hygiene habits, and systemic health. Diffuse hair thinning can indicate endocrine disorders or severe nutritional deficiencies, while patchy hair loss may point to localized fungal infections or autoimmune conditions.

headings.title: Routine Hygiene and Shampooing Techniques
headings.content: Routine hair cleansing removes dirt, sweat, dead skin cells, and excess sebum. For hospitalized or bedridden patients, nurses utilize specialized inflatable shampoo basins or dry shampoo caps to maintain hygiene without causing discomfort. Water temperature must be checked carefully before application to prevent thermal burns. Massaging the scalp gently with the pads of the fingers—never the fingernails—stimulates local blood circulation and prevents trauma to the delicate scalp epithelium.

headings.title: Managing Special Hair Care Needs
headings.content: Patients with textured, coiled, or tightly curled hair require specific care approaches to prevent breakage and dryness. Unlike straight hair, the natural oils from the scalp travel less easily down coiled hair shafts, making these hair types naturally drier. Wide-toothed combs, detangling from ends to roots, and protective moisturizing products help maintain hair integrity. For patients with physical limitations or long-term bedrest, daily gentle brushing and systematic braiding can prevent severe matting and tangling.

headings.title: Prevention and Management of Common Scalp Conditions
headings.content: Common scalp conditions encountered in clinical settings include dandruff, pediculosis capitis (head lice), and seborrheic dermatitis. Dandruff involves flaking and mild itching without significant inflammation, managed well with medicated anti-dandruff shampoos containing zinc pyrithione or selenium sulfide. Pediculosis requires treating both the affected individual and household contacts with appropriate pediculicides, followed by meticulous removal of nits with a fine-toothed comb.

headings.title: Documentation and Patient Education
headings.content: Nursing documentation regarding hair and scalp care must be accurate and objective. Nurses should record the condition of the scalp, presence of any lesions, hygiene measures performed, and the patient's tolerance of the procedure. Patient education focuses on teaching proper hygiene habits, avoiding harsh chemical treatments, and recognizing early signs of infection or unusual hair loss. Empowering patients with self-care knowledge promotes long-term dermatological health.
